tagline: A former primary highway links Green Bay with the Farmville area
intro: Route 696 connects US 360 at Green Bay with US 460 southeast of Farmville, entirely within Prince Edward County. Nearby, the Sandy River runs north through Prince Edward State Forest and farmland toward the Bush River.

The road entered the state highway system in stages: 5.5 miles from Green Bay in 1930, another half-mile in 1931, and the remaining six miles in 1932. Initially SR 318, it became SR 135 in the 1933 renumbering, then a secondary road in 1945.

Driving south follows the former primary route from the Farmville end at US 460 to Green Bay on US 360. Sandy River Reservoir lies east of Farmville and south of Rice. Near Green Bay, Twin Lakes State Park offers a separate excursion to the former Goodwin Lake and Prince Edward Lake parks.

moments.title: Sandy River Reservoir
moments.text: This 740-acre reservoir east of Farmville was built to supply water. Construction finished in 1994, and fishing opened in 1996. Prince Edward County owns the reservoir; the Virginia Department of Game and Inland Fisheries was assigned responsibility for managing its fisheries.

moments.title: Twin Lakes State Park
moments.text: Twin Lakes includes a park Virginia created for African Americans while continuing to deny them entry to another state park. In 1948, authorities at Staunton River State Park turned away Maceo Conrad Martin and his family because of their race. The civil rights firm Hill, Tucker and Robinson sued the Commonwealth on their behalf. Virginia funded separate facilities, and Prince Edward State Park for Negroes opened in June 1950. A state historical marker explains that Governor William M. Tuck funded the park in lieu of access. African Americans came from across the mid-Atlantic states for swimming, camping, recreation and dancing.

moments.title: Green Bay
moments.text: Green Bay sits on US 360 between Burkeville and Keysville. Peach growing flourished here in the 1930s and 1940s, then declined as larger growers advanced and techniques and labor availability changed. The community had rail access through a Norfolk and Western mainline and the Southern Railway. The former SR 135 ran north from this US 360 connection toward Farmville along present SR 696.
